title: The GPCC Drought Index – a new, combined and gridded global drought index
abstract: Abstract. The Global Precipitation Climatology Centre Drought Index (GPCC-DI) provides estimations of water supply anomalies with respect to long-term statistics. It is a combination of the Standardized Precipitation Index with adaptations from Deutscher Wetterdienst (SPI-DWD) and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Precipitation data were taken from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) and temperature data from NOAA's Climate Prediction Center (CPC). The GPCC-DI is available with several accumulation periods of 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 24 and 48 months for different applications. It is issued monthly starting in January 2013. Typically, it is released on the 10th day of the following month, depending on the availability of the input data. It is calculated on a regular grid with 1° spatial resolution. All accumulation periods are integrated into one netCDF file for each month. This data set is referenced by the doi:10.5676/DWD_GPCC/DI_M_100 and is available free of charge from the GPCC website ftp://ftp.dwd.de/pub/data/gpcc/html/gpcc_di_doi_download.html.
problem: Existing drought indices suffer from individual shortcomings, such as ignoring temperature effects or being undefined in cold/arid regions, which prevents any single index from providing a timely, reliable, and comprehensive assessment of drought on a global scale.
method: The authors propose a new, combined, and gridded global drought index (GPCC-DI) that estimates water supply anomalies by calculating the mean of the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-DWD) and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) to achieve nearly global coverage.
task: The task is to present a new, combined, and gridded global drought index (GPCC-DI) based on precipitation and temperature data for monitoring water supply anomalies with respect to long-term statistics.
innovation: This paper introduces the GPCC Drought Index, a new, combined, and gridded global drought index created by integrating the Standardized Precipitation Index and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index to provide nearly global monthly monitoring of water supply anomalies.

Drought indices are a measure of the anomalies of available water with respect to long-term statistics. They can be based on station as well as on grid data, such as precipitation, temperature, wind speed, radiation and evaporation, but also on non-meteorological data, such as soil type, soil moisture or ground water level. It is common to classify three main conditions: drought, normal and wet. Drought conditions are refined as moderate, severe and extreme drought (Palmer, 1965).
